docs.title: OpsSignal
docs.text:
A Rust-powered SDK for turning application and workflow events into structured, routed operational notifications: Slack, webhooks, and more, from a single event model.

Status: beta (latest release v1.0.0-beta.1)

Config keys, the Python API and the SQLite schema may still change before 1.0.0. The most-tested integration targets are Airflow and dbt, via the Python bindings. The CLI and a C ABI (for future Java/Go bindings) exist but are young.

Which release has which feature

Use the version picker at the top to read the docs for the release you installed; latest is the newest release and dev is the unreleased main branch. Within a version, features newer than v1.0.0-beta.1 carry an "Added in" note naming the release that brings them. See Releases for what changed in each version.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Application or workflow event] --> B[Rust core<br/>validate, route, deliver, record]
    B --> C[Console]
    B --> D[Slack]
    B --> E[Webhook]
    B --> G[PagerDuty]
    B --> H[Microsoft Teams]
    B -.-> F[(SQLite sink)]

Existing tools solve parts of this problem. Alertmanager routes alerts but isn't an embeddable application SDK, Airflow callbacks are Python-only, and Slack or Teams SDKs are provider-specific. OpsSignal combines a shared Rust core, a common signal model and a provider abstraction, so the same routing and retry logic behaves the same way from every calling language.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text: OpsSignal is not an event bus, message queue or workflow orchestrator. It does not do event sourcing, complex event processing or long-running scheduling. It sits downstream of those systems and turns their events into notifications.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This document records the design decisions for opssignal and the trade-offs behind them. If you're implementing a new provider, sink, or binding, read this first.

The Python and FFI bindings each hold one process-global SignalClient, built lazily from signal.yaml on the first call. The CLI builds one per invocation.

docs.title: Lifecycle of one signal
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Caller
    participant Client as SignalClient
    participant Router as RoutingConfig
    participant Provider
    participant Sink as SqliteSink

    App->>Client: notify_async(input)
    Client->>Client: validate, assign id + timestamp + dedup key
    Client->>Sink: record(signal), status pending
    Client-->>App: returns
    Client->>Router: plan(signal)
    Router-->>Client: delivery targets (never empty, console fallback)
    par each target, concurrently
        loop each provider of the target until one succeeds
            Client->>Sink: provider_outcome(pending)
            Client->>Provider: send(signal), up to 3 attempts with backoff
            Provider-->>Client: Ok / Err
            Client->>Sink: provider_outcome(delivered / failed)
        end
    end
    Client->>Sink: complete(signal, delivery result)

notify_sync runs the same steps but blocks the caller until the result is known or the timeout expires.

A delivery plan is a list of targets, each an ordered list of providers. A failover route's providers join the one shared failover target; each provider of a fanout route is a target of its own. Targets run concurrently and never share retries, so a provider that delivered is never sent the signal again because another provider failed. The overall status is delivered (every target succeeded), partial (some did) or failed. A config without fanout has a single target and behaves exactly as it did before delivery modes existed.

Routes that set dedup or rate_limit are checked while the plan is built, on the caller's thread, so repeats are judged in the order they were sent. A route held back adds no providers; if every matching route was held back, the plan is empty and the signal is stored as skipped (the console fallback is only for signals that match nothing). The history is a throttle table in the sink's SQLite file, written inside an IMMEDIATE transaction, so every process on a host that shares the file sees the same windows. A send that ends failed is removed again so it can't suppress the next occurrence. Any error reading the history lets the signal through. Coordinating across hosts is deliberately not part of the embedded SDK.

notify_async callers wait only for the local sink write, never for a provider. Its deliveries run on the client's runtime, so a process that exits would cut them off. SignalClient::flush(timeout) waits for them, and every binding calls it on the way out: dropping a Rust SignalClient flushes for up to 5 seconds, the Python package registers flush() with atexit, and C hosts call signal_flush(timeout_ms) before exiting (the library holds a process-global client that is never dropped). The CLI uses notify_sync, so it has nothing in flight. A signal still undelivered when the wait runs out stays in the sink as pending.

docs.title: Signal model
docs.text:
pub struct Signal {
    pub id: Uuid,              // core-generated, never caller-supplied
    pub source: String,
    pub event_type: String,
    pub severity: Severity,    // closed enum, not a free string
    pub title: String,
    pub message: Option<String>,
    pub environment: Option<String>,
    pub metadata: serde_json::Value,
    pub timestamp: DateTime<Utc>,  // core-stamped
    pub dedup_key: Option<String>, // computed if caller omits it
    // ...
}

id and timestamp are always core-generated. Every downstream component (sink, dedup, retry tracking) needs a stable identity and ordering guarantee that doesn't depend on every language binding remembering to set these correctly.

docs.title: Delivery semantics: sync vs async
docs.text:
Both notify_sync and notify_async share one internal pipeline (validate → record → route → deliver → complete). The only difference is whether the calling thread blocks on the delivery future.

Default for the Airflow adapter is async (fire-and-forget). A blocking call on a flaky Slack webhook inside an on_failure_callback would add latency and a new failure mode to the very DAG run being monitored. Callers who want a delivery guarantee can call notify_sync directly with an explicit timeout.

The design rule is that persistence to the sink happens before delivery is attempted, regardless of sync/async: the signal is stored as pending, then updated to delivered or failed. A failed delivery is durably recorded, and a signal whose process died mid-delivery is still visible as pending rather than lost. This is what makes delivery analytics and MTTR reporting possible later without re-architecting.

A sink error never stops delivery. If record fails it is logged and the signal is delivered anyway; complete writes the whole row, so the outcome still lands if the sink has recovered.

docs.title: The storage boundary
docs.text:
pub trait SignalSink: Send + Sync {
    /// Before delivery: store the signal as pending.
    fn record(&self, signal: &Signal) -> Result<(), SignalError>;
    /// After delivery: store the outcome (an upsert; must work without `record`).
    fn complete(&self, signal: &Signal, result: &DeliveryResult) -> Result<(), SignalError>;
    /// During delivery: one provider's outcome, pending then delivered/failed.
    /// Optional; defaults to doing nothing.
    fn provider_outcome(&self, signal: &Signal, outcome: &ProviderOutcome) -> Result<(), SignalError>;
}

A sink is a write-only side effect, not a queryable API. This SDK does not expose querying, dashboards, or aggregation — that's explicitly out of scope for the open-source core (see "what this is not" in the README) and is the hosted control plane's job, reading from the same SQLite/Postgres file OSS users already populate.

  • SQLite is the default sink: zero-config, works out of the box.
  • Postgres / S3 are opt-in for centralized analytics across multiple workers — relevant once you outgrow a single-node Airflow deployment, since SQLite's single-writer model will start serializing writes under concurrent load.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
Routing config matches signals against rules and resolves to a list of provider names.

Invariant: unmatched signals always fall back to the console provider. A signal that matches no route must never silently disappear — that failure mode is worse than not having the SDK at all. This is enforced in RoutingConfig::resolve, not left to configuration.

docs.title: Config sources and reload
docs.text:
SIGNAL_CONFIG can name a local file, an https://, s3://, gs:// or az:// object, an AWS AppConfig profile (appconfig://), an Azure App Configuration key (azappconfig://), or one item of DynamoDB (dynamodb://), Firestore (firestore://) or Cosmos DB (cosmos://) (crates/core/src/source.rs). The cloud code lives in crates/core/src/cloud/, one module per cloud, and non-storage services are signed with the credentials object_store already resolves (SigV4 on AWS; Entra tokens for the service's own audience on Azure), so no cloud SDK is in the tree. The cloud stores sit behind the aws, gcp and azure cargo features of opssignal-core, so the core stays light. They run on the same reqwest/rustls stack as the providers rather than pulling in a second one.

Cloud code ships only in cloud packages. The base CLI and C library compile none of it; their aws, gcp, azure and all features build a variant that is the base plus that cloud. The Python wheel compiles none either: each cloud ships as its own wheel (crates/python-aws, -gcp, -azure), installed through the opssignal[aws], [gcp] and [azure] extras, because pip extras can add packages but cannot change what is compiled into one. At startup the base binding imports whichever add-ons are installed and registers each one's fetch with the core for every scheme of its cloud (source::register_cloud_fetcher). The core calls it on a plain thread for that scheme, with the same cache and fallback rules. An add-on is a thin wrapper around source::fetch_blocking; it has no logic of its own.

Two reliability rules shape this code:

  • A config source is never a reason to lose a signal. A remote source that is unreachable or serves a broken file falls back to the last good cached copy, then to the zero-config default (console only). The cache holds the raw text before ${VAR} substitution, so it never contains secrets. ${aws-sm:...}, ${gcp-sm:...} and ${azure-kv:...} placeholders are resolved by secrets.rs after each file is fetched (values cached in memory for SIGNAL_SECRETS_TTL_SECS); a store that can't be reached is handled like an unreachable source.
  • A reload is all or nothing. reload.rs polls the source on an interval (default 60 s) and, when the text or a fingerprint of its resolved secrets changes and loads cleanly, swaps routes and providers together as one Pipeline behind an RwLock<Arc<_>>. In-flight deliveries keep the Arc they started with. A failed reload keeps the current pipeline. The sink is never reopened live.

A config can be layered: a file may extends: others, and SIGNAL_CONFIG may list several (crates/core/src/chain.rs). The chain is walked depth first into a list of files, lowest priority first, with each file loaded once, cycles rejected, and a depth (8) and file (64) limit. Config::from_layers merges it: providers by name, later routes first, storage from the last file that sets it. Routes are checked only after the merge. Each remote file is cached on its own, and the reloader re-walks the whole chain on every poll and compares the texts of every file, so a change to a shared default reaches all the teams that extend it. A remote file may not extend a local path.

Polling is used instead of filesystem notifications because Kubernetes updates ConfigMap mounts by swapping a symlink, which file watchers often miss, and the same loop covers remote sources.

docs.title: FFI panic safety
docs.text:
Every #[no_mangle] extern "C" function in crates/ffi must be wrapped in catch_unwind (see crates/ffi/src/lib.rs::guarded). A Rust panic crossing the FFI boundary is undefined behavior in the host language and can crash the calling process outright — for an embedded SDK, that's worse than the failure it was supposed to report on.

The Python bindings (crates/python) additionally translate Result::Err into real Python exceptions via PyO3 — never a silently swallowed None.

docs.title: Why two separate Rust crates for bindings (ffi vs python)
docs.text: crates/ffi is a generic C ABI layer intended for future Java/Go bindings via JNI/cgo. crates/python uses PyO3 macros directly, which is a different (and for Python, more idiomatic and lower-overhead) binding mechanism than hand-rolled C ABI. Both wrap the same opssignal-core logic; neither contains business logic of its own.

docs.title: What's deliberately out of scope
docs.text:
• Event bus / message queue semantics
  • Event sourcing, complex event processing
  • Long-running workflow orchestration
  • Java and Go bindings (designed for, not built — see roadmap in README)
  • Querying/dashboards over stored signals (hosted control plane territory)

docs.title: Revisit triggers
docs.text: Decision Revisit when Embedded Tokio runtime If embedding conflicts with host apps that have their own async runtime become common SQLite default sink When users run multi-worker Airflow and need unified cross-worker history No bounded buffering/backpressure If burst scenarios (thousands of signals in a tight loop) overwhelm provider rate limits Hash-based dedup If semantically-identical-but-textually-different signals need correlation (likely an AI-correlation premium feature, not OSS core)

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
All notable changes to OpsSignal are listed here, newest first. The format follows Keep a Changelog and versions follow Semantic Versioning. Pre-releases (-beta.N) may still change config keys, the Python API and the SQLite schema.

The Python packages use PEP 440 spelling for the same version, so 1.0.0-beta.1 is 1.0.0b1 on PyPI.

docs.title: Unreleased
docs.text: Changes merged to main that are not in a release yet. They will ship in the next tag.

docs.title: 1.0.0-beta.2 - 2026-10-21
docs.text: Second beta: send one signal to several places at once, shape each provider's message, and keep noisy routes quiet. Configs written for 1.0.0-beta.1 keep working unchanged, except that a misspelled key inside a route's match is now reported instead of silently matching everything.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Fan-out delivery: a route can set mode: fanout to deliver to every provider it lists at once, each retried on its own, so a provider that already got the signal is never sent it again because another failed. failover stays the default. A fan-out that reaches only some providers is reported as partial, with each provider's result, and the CLI exits 1 (#26).
  • Message templates per provider: an optional template block under any provider replaces parts of its message with Jinja text, such as Slack's text, PagerDuty's summary, Teams' title/text, Opsgenie's message/description, email's subject/body, console's line, or the whole webhook JSON body. Templates see every signal field plus metadata.*. Syntax errors, unknown parts and unknown variables fail at load time; a template that fails at send time falls back to the built-in format, so the alert still goes out. Configs without templates send exactly what they did before. Python and the C library get this from the config, with no API change (#32).
  • opssignal preview prints what each provider would be sent for a signal, without sending or recording it, and opssignal notify/preview take --metadata as a JSON object (#32).
  • Dedup and rate limits per route: dedup: 30m sends each incident (dedup key) at most once per window, and rate_limit: {max: 10, per: 1h} caps how many signals a route sends. Held-back signals are stored with status skipped. The history lives in the SQLite file, so it holds across processes on one host (cron, Airflow tasks, the CLI) and across restarts. A failed send never suppresses the next one. The CLI exits 0 for a suppressed signal and prints the reason (#31).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Rust API: ConsoleProvider is now a struct built with ConsoleProvider::new(), the Provider trait has a preview method with a default, so existing implementations still compile, and DeliveryResult gains a Partial status with per-provider results.
  • The SQLite sink keeps one deliveries row per signal and provider, so a signal's history shows which providers already have it.
  • PyPI pages for opssignal, opssignal-aws, opssignal-gcp and opssignal-azure get a project description, links, keywords and classifiers (#25). PyPI fixes a version's metadata at its first upload, so this shows from the next release; the 1.0.0b1 pages stay without a description.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text: • An unknown key inside a route's match (such as enviroment: prod) is now a load-time error. It used to be ignored, so the route matched every signal (#31).

docs.title: 1.0.0-beta.1 - 2026-10-20
docs.text: First public build, published to PyPI (pip install --pre opssignal) and crates.io (opssignal-core, opssignal-cli).

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Providers: Slack, Microsoft Teams, PagerDuty (Events API v2), Opsgenie, email (SMTP, or Amazon SES with opssignal[aws]), generic webhook and console. A route lists providers in order and delivery stops at the first one that succeeds, so later providers are fallbacks. Each provider gets up to 3 attempts with backoff.
  • Config sources: local file, https://, s3://, gs://, az://, AWS AppConfig (appconfig://), Azure App Configuration (azappconfig://), and DynamoDB, Firestore and Cosmos DB items.
  • Live reload every 60 seconds (SIGNAL_CONFIG_REFRESH_SECS); a broken edit is logged and skipped. Remote configs are cached locally and used when the source is unreachable.
  • Layered configs with extends: or a comma-separated SIGNAL_CONFIG list: a platform default file plus per-team files.
  • Secrets: ${VAR}, ${aws-sm:...}, ${gcp-sm:...} and ${azure-kv:...} references, cached in memory only.
  • Reliability: every signal is stored in SQLite as pending before delivery, then marked delivered or failed. In-flight signals are flushed on exit (Rust drop, Python atexit, C signal_flush).
  • Python: notify() with full signal context, an Airflow failure_callback, and a dbt adapter (run_results.json or a dbtRunner callback).
  • CLI: opssignal notify, which exits non-zero when an alert was not delivered.
  • C ABI in crates/ffi for C hosts and future bindings.
  • Packaging: a cloud-free base package with opssignal[aws], [gcp], [azure] and [all] extras, and matching cargo features for the CLI and C library. abi3 wheels for Python 3.9+ on Linux (glibc and musl, x86_64 and aarch64), Windows x86_64 and macOS arm64 (the macOS wheel was added to 1.0.0b1 on 2026-10-21). The Rust crates need Rust 1.89+.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• No fan-out: to send one signal to two places, use two routes.
  • Signals left pending or failed are kept but not redelivered later.
  • SQLite is the only sink; a team config file can add routes but not remove inherited ones.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text: The opssignal binary sends a signal from a shell, CI job or cron entry. It uses the same Rust core, config and routing as the Python package.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: cargo install --path crates/cli

docs.title: opssignal notify
docs.text:
opssignal notify \
  --source ci \
  --event-type build_failed \
  --severity error \
  --title "main is red" \
  --message "3 tests failed" \
  --environment prod
Flag Required Default Notes --source yes Where the event came from, such as ci or airflow. --event-type yes What happened, such as build_failed. --title yes One-line summary. Must not be blank. --severity no info info, success, warning, error or critical (case-insensitive). --message no Longer detail. --environment no Used by routes that match on environment. --metadata no A JSON object, such as '{"dag_id": "orders"}', for templates to use. Added in v1.0.0-beta.2. --config no Path to a config file. Overrides $SIGNAL_CONFIG and ./signal.yaml.

Unlike the Python notify(), the CLI waits for delivery, with a 5 second timeout, so a CI step can fail when an alert didn't go out.

docs.title: opssignal preview
docs.text:
Added in v1.0.0-beta.2

Prints what each provider would be sent, for checking message templates.

opssignal preview \
  --source airflow \
  --event-type task_failed \
  --severity error \
  --title "load failed" \
  --metadata '{"dag_id": "orders"}'

Takes the same flags as notify, plus --provider NAME to show one provider whether or not a route picks it. Prints a JSON list of {"provider": ..., "payload": ...} in delivery order. Nothing is sent and nothing is recorded. Credentials in a payload, such as PagerDuty's routing_key, are shown as <redacted>. Email's payload is its subject and body. Exits 2 on bad input, a config that fails to load, or a --provider that isn't configured.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Delivered, or held back by a route's dedup or rate_limit (stderr then shows suppressed: ... with the reason). 1 Delivery failed or timed out, or a fanout route reached only some of its providers. The outcome is still recorded in the sink, and stderr lists each provider's result. 2 Bad input (blank title, unknown severity) or a config that fails to load.

Errors are printed to stderr as error: ....

docs.title: Where the config comes from
docs.text:
OpsSignal looks for its config in this order:

  1. The SIGNAL_CONFIG environment variable. It can be a local path or a URL:

    Value Source Notes /etc/opssignal/signal.yaml local file Must exist, or loading fails. https://config.example.com/signal.yaml HTTPS GET Plain http:// is accepted only for localhost. s3://bucket/path/signal.yaml Amazon S3 (or any S3-compatible store) Python: opssignal[aws]. gs://bucket/path/signal.yaml Google Cloud Storage Python: opssignal[gcp]. az://container/path/signal.yaml Azure Blob Storage Python: opssignal[azure]. Set AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME to the storage account. appconfig://application/environment/profile AWS AppConfig Python: opssignal[aws]. See Managed config services. azappconfig://store/key?label=prod Azure App Configuration Python: opssignal[azure]. ?label= is optional. dynamodb://table/id Amazon DynamoDB item Python: opssignal[aws]. See Databases. firestore://project/collection/document Firestore document Python: opssignal[gcp]. cosmos://account/database/container/id Azure Cosmos DB item Python: opssignal[azure].

  2. ./signal.yaml in the current working directory.

  3. Nothing found: the zero-config default (console provider, SQLite sink at ./signals.db).

SIGNAL_CONFIG can also list several files, separated by commas, which are merged as described in Layered configs. The CLI also accepts --config <path or URL> (or a comma-separated list), which overrides both.

docs.title: Installing cloud support
docs.text:
pip install opssignal reads local files and HTTPS only. Each cloud is a pip extra that installs a small native add-on, which opssignal finds on its own:

Install Adds pip install 'opssignal[aws]' s3://, appconfig://, dynamodb://, ${aws-sm:...} secrets, email through the SES API pip install 'opssignal[gcp]' gs://, firestore://, ${gcp-sm:...} secrets pip install 'opssignal[azure]' az://, azappconfig://, cosmos://, ${azure-kv:...} secrets pip install 'opssignal[all]' all three

If SIGNAL_CONFIG names a cloud whose extra isn't installed, the first notify() raises RuntimeError naming the extra to install (the CLI exits with code 2 and names the feature to build with). That is treated as a setup mistake, so it fails straight away instead of falling back.

The CLI and the C library follow the same rule: the base build reads local files and HTTPS only, and each cloud is added on top of it with a cargo feature named like the pip extra:

Build Adds cargo build -p opssignal-cli --features aws s3://, appconfig://, dynamodb://, ${aws-sm:...}, email through the SES API cargo build -p opssignal-cli --features gcp gs://, firestore://, ${gcp-sm:...} cargo build -p opssignal-cli --features azure az://, azappconfig://, cosmos://, ${azure-kv:...} cargo build -p opssignal-cli --features all all three

The same features exist on opssignal-ffi for the C library. If you depend on the opssignal-core crate directly, the features are aws, gcp and azure; without them the core reads files and HTTPS only.

docs.title: Remote configs
docs.text:
One signal.yaml in a bucket can serve every service. Each process sets SIGNAL_CONFIG to the same URL and keeps its secrets in its own environment (see Environment variables in values), so the shared file never holds a token.

Credentials. OpsSignal uses each platform's standard credential chain and has no keys of its own:

  • S3: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, web identity (EKS IRSA), ECS task roles, or the EC2 instance profile. Set AWS_REGION to the bucket's region. AWS_ENDPOINT_URL points it at MinIO or another S3-compatible store.
  • GCS: GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS or GOOGLE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT, gcloud application-default credentials, then the metadata server (GKE workload identity, GCE service accounts).
  • Azure: AKS workload identity (AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE, set by the workload identity webhook), managed identity, a service principal (AZURE_CLIENT_ID/AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET/AZURE_TENANT_ID), a SAS token (AZURE_STORAGE_SAS_KEY) or an account key.
  • HTTPS: no authentication; use a URL that is reachable only from your network, or a pre-signed URL.

The process only needs read access to that one object (s3:GetObject, storage.objects.get, or the Storage Blob Data Reader role on Azure).

docs.title: Managed config services
docs.text:
AWS AppConfig and Azure App Configuration hold the same YAML as a file, and add change control a bucket doesn't have. AppConfig validates a change before it goes live, rolls it out gradually with a deployment strategy, and rolls it back automatically on a CloudWatch alarm. App Configuration keeps a label per environment, a revision history and snapshots, so a bad edit can be restored to an earlier value. Each team's file is one profile or key, and extends: works between them:

# appconfig://opssignal/prod/payments
extends: default          # the "default" profile of the same application and environment

# azappconfig://ops-config/opssignal/teams/payments?label=prod
extends: ../default       # key opssignal/default, same store and label
AWS AppConfig Azure App Configuration URL appconfig://<application>/<environment>/<profile> (names or IDs) azappconfig://<store>/<key>[?label=<label>] Credentials The AWS chain above Workload identity, service principal or managed identity, as above Permissions appconfig:StartConfigurationSession, appconfig:GetLatestConfiguration App Configuration Data Reader Endpoint override AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_APPCONFIGDATA AZURE_APPCONFIG_ENDPOINT, with {store} in it, for sovereign clouds

What polling costs. AppConfig bills for each configuration it sends, so OpsSignal keeps its polling session between checks: an unchanged profile returns an empty, unbilled answer. App Configuration is asked with the last ETag, so an unchanged key costs a request but no download. Each check is still one request per file per process, which matters on App Configuration's request quotas when thousands of pods poll: raise SIGNAL_CONFIG_REFRESH_SECS there if needed.

Cache and fallback. After every successful fetch, the raw file is cached on local disk, before ${VAR} substitution, so no secret is ever written there. When the source can't be reached, times out (10 seconds), or returns a file that fails to load, OpsSignal uses the last good cached copy. If there is no cached copy either, it starts on the zero-config default (console only) and logs why, so a bucket outage never stops a service from starting or sending signals. It switches to the real config as soon as the source is back.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
Use a database when teams change their own routing through an internal UI or API instead of pull requests: the tool writes each team's YAML into one item, and OpsSignal reads it like a file. Writes, change history (DynamoDB Streams, the Cosmos DB change feed, Firestore triggers) and access control stay in the database. OpsSignal only ever reads.

Each item holds the whole YAML of one file in a single string attribute, config by default:

DynamoDB Firestore Cosmos DB URL dynamodb://<table>/<id> firestore://<project>/<collection>/<document> (nested paths allowed) cosmos://<account>/<database>/<container>/<id> Item lookup String partition key id (?key= to rename); tables with a sort key are not supported Document path; ?database= for a non-default database Item id; partition key value is the id, or ?pk= YAML attribute config (?value= to rename) string field config (?field=) string property config (?field=) Permissions dynamodb:GetItem datastore.entities.get (Cloud Datastore Viewer) Cosmos DB Built-in Data Reader (data-plane RBAC; account keys are not used) Endpoint override AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_DYNAMODB (DynamoDB Local) FIRESTORE_EMULATOR_HOST AZURE_COSMOS_ENDPOINT, with {account} in it

extends: names another item of the same table, database or container:

# dynamodb://opssignal-config/payments
extends: default          # item "default" of the same table

In Firestore a relative entry resolves like a path (../shared/db-alerts from opssignal/payments). In Cosmos DB the parent's partition key value is taken to be its id; use a full cosmos:// URL with ?pk= otherwise.

Each check is one read per file per process: an eventually consistent GetItem (half a read unit), one Firestore document read, or one Cosmos DB point read (sent with the last ETag, so an unchanged item is a 304).

docs.title: Live reload
docs.text:
The config is re-read every 60 seconds and changes are applied without a restart, for local files and remote sources alike. A change replaces the routes and providers as one unit, so no signal sees new routes with old providers.

A reload that can't be fetched or fails to load is skipped and logged, and the current config stays in place. A broken edit can't take alerting down.

Changes to storage are not applied live, because reopening the sink under traffic could lose writes. They are logged and take effect on the next restart.

Variable Default Effect SIGNAL_CONFIG_REFRESH_SECS 60 Seconds between checks. 0 loads once and never reloads. SIGNAL_CONFIG_CACHE_DIR $XDG_CACHE_HOME/opssignal, else ~/.cache/opssignal Where remote configs are cached.

The CLI sends one signal and exits, so it loads the config once.

See Kubernetes for a ConfigMap and Secret setup that uses live reload.

docs.title: Layered configs
docs.text:
Large organisations rarely keep every route in one file. OpsSignal lets a file build on others, so a platform team can own a default and each team adds only what is its own:

# default.yaml, owned by the platform team
providers:
  slack:
    webhook_url: "${ORG_SLACK_WEBHOOK}"
routes:
  - match: { severity: [error, critical] }
    providers: [slack]
storage:
  path: /var/lib/opssignal/signals.db

# teams/payments.yaml
extends: ../default.yaml
providers:
  webhook:
    url: "${PAYMENTS_PAGER_URL}"
routes:
  - match: { source: payments, severity: [critical] }
    providers: [webhook, slack]

Point SIGNAL_CONFIG at the team file and the default comes with it.

There are two ways to combine files, and they can be mixed:

  • extends: in a file names one parent, or a list of them. A relative entry is resolved against the file's own location: the same directory, or the same bucket or container for s3://, gs:// and az://, or the same site for https://. A URL or an absolute path is used as is.
  • A list in SIGNAL_CONFIG, such as SIGNAL_CONFIG=teams/payments.yaml,shared/db-alerts.yaml. Use this when a service needs alerts that several teams share, without one team file having to name another.

Files are merged lowest priority first: parents before the file that extends them, and earlier entries of a list before later ones. A file reached more than once, such as a default that every team extends, is loaded once.

Section How it merges providers By name. A later file's slack, webhook, pagerduty, teams or console replaces the earlier one whole. routes Added together. A later file's routes go first, so the more specific file is matched first and its providers are tried first, while the inherited routes still catch everything else. storage Taken from the last file that sets it.

Because a failover route stops at the first provider that succeeds (see delivery modes), a team route that matches a signal effectively decides where it goes, and the inherited failover providers become its fallbacks. An inherited fanout route still delivers to all of its providers. Routes are checked after merging, so a team file can route to a provider that only its parent configures. A route naming an unknown provider is reported with the file it is in, such as teams/payments.yaml: routes[0] references provider 'pagerduty'.

Rules that keep chains manageable:

  • A cycle (a.yaml extends b.yaml, which extends a.yaml) is a load-time error that shows the loop.
  • A chain can be at most 8 files deep and load at most 64 files.
  • A remote file can extend other remote files but not local paths, so a file served over the network can never read the host's disk. A local file can extend a remote one, such as a team ConfigMap that extends a default in a bucket.

Every file in the chain is reloaded and cached on its own. An edit to the default reaches every team on the next check. When a remote file can't be fetched, its cached copy is used; if the fresh files load but no longer fit together (a team routes to a provider someone just removed from the default), the cached copies of the whole chain are used instead. Only if neither works does OpsSignal start on the zero-config default. A missing or broken local file in the chain stops loading, as a single local file does.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
providers:
  slack:
    webhook_url: "${SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL}"
  webhook:
    url: "https://ops.example.com/hooks/opssignal"

routes:
  - match:
      severity: [error, critical]
      environment: prod
    providers: [slack]
  - match:
      source: ci
    providers: [webhook]

storage:
  sink: sqlite
  path: "./signals.db"

signal.yaml is gitignored in this repository. Commit only files that use ${VAR} placeholders for secrets, like python/examples/signal.example.yaml.

docs.title: providers
docs.text:
Key Fields Notes console enabled (optional) Always registered, because it is the routing fallback. It cannot be turned off. slack webhook_url Slack incoming-webhook URL. webhook url Receives the full signal as a JSON POST. pagerduty routing_key, url (optional) Triggers a PagerDuty alert through the Events API v2. url defaults to the US endpoint; EU accounts set https://events.eu.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue. teams webhook_url Microsoft Teams Workflows (or legacy incoming) webhook URL. Posts an Adaptive Card.

Providers describes what each one sends and how to get its URL or key.

Added in v1.0.0-beta.2

Any provider can also set template, which replaces parts of the message it sends; see Message templates.

Unknown provider keys are rejected, so a typo such as slak: fails at load time instead of silently dropping a provider.

docs.title: routes
docs.text:
Each route has a match block and a list of providers. Every condition in match must hold; an omitted condition matches anything.

Field Type Matches when severity list of info, success, warning, error, critical the signal's severity is in the list environment string the signal's environment equals it source string the signal's source equals it

A route can also set mode, which decides what its list of providers means:

Field Values Default mode failover, fanout failover

docs.title: Delivery modes
docs.text:
Added in v1.0.0-beta.2

mode: fanout. Before it, every route behaved as failover.

failover (the default): the providers are tried in order and delivery stops at the first one that succeeds. Each provider gets up to 3 attempts with exponential backoff before the next one is tried. Later providers are fallbacks, not extra copies.

fanout: the signal goes to every provider in the list at the same time. Each provider is retried on its own (up to 3 attempts), so a failing PagerDuty never causes a second Slack message, and a slow provider never holds up the others.

routes:
  # Page on-call and tell the channel, every time.
  - match:
      severity: [critical]
      environment: prod
    providers: [pagerduty, slack]
    mode: fanout
  # Everything else: Teams, or email if Teams is down.
  - match: {}
    providers: [teams, email]

When several routes match one signal:

  • each provider of a matching fanout route is delivered to on its own;
  • the providers of all matching failover routes form one ordered list (in file order), which is delivered to alongside the fan-out providers and stops at its first success, exactly as before fanout existed;
  • a provider named by more than one matching route is used once, at its first position, so it never receives the same signal twice.

In the example above, a critical prod signal goes to PagerDuty, Slack, and Teams (falling back to email); any other signal goes to Teams, falling back to email.

The outcome is delivered when every fan-out provider and the failover list succeeded, failed when none did, and partial when some did. The sink keeps each provider's result too; see storage.

If no route matches, the list is just console. That fallback is built into the routing engine and cannot be configured away.

docs.title: Dedup and rate limits
docs.text:
Added in v1.0.0-beta.2

Routes can set dedup and rate_limit.

A failing job that retries every minute, or one bad deploy that breaks 200 DAGs, should page once, not hundreds of times. Two optional route fields hold back the repeats:

Field Value Effect dedup a window: 30s, 10m, 2h, 1d (a bare number is seconds) The route sends each dedup key at most once per window. Repeats inside the window are suppressed. rate_limit {max: N, per: <window>} The route sends at most N signals in any sliding per window, whatever their key. Signals over the limit are suppressed. 
routes:
  # One page per incident every 30 minutes, and never more than 10 pages
  # an hour even if every DAG fails at once.
  - match:
      severity: [critical]
      environment: prod
    providers: [pagerduty, slack]
    mode: fanout
    dedup: 30m
    rate_limit:
      max: 10
      per: 1h
  # The channel still gets every warning, unthrottled.
  - match:
      severity: [warning, error]
    providers: [slack]

How they behave:

  • Per route. A suppressed route adds none of its providers for that signal; other matching routes still send. To page once but keep every occurrence in a channel, give the paging route a dedup and add an unthrottled route for the channel.
  • The window starts at the last send, not the last repeat, so a long-running incident re-alerts once per dedup window as a reminder.
  • Only sends count. A suppressed signal does not use up the rate_limit, and a signal that no provider delivered (status failed) is taken back, so the next occurrence is tried again instead of being suppressed as a duplicate of an alert nobody received.
  • Suppressed signals are still recorded in the sink with status skipped and the reason in error, for example route [pagerduty, slack]: duplicate of a signal sent 4m ago (dedup 30m). If a signal was suppressed on one route and delivered on another, its status is the delivered one.
  • Shared by every process on the host that uses the same storage.path: the history is kept in that SQLite file, so a CLI run from cron, each Airflow task process and a restarted service all see the same windows. Hosts do not share it with each other.
  • Editing a route (its match, providers, mode or limits) starts its history afresh.
  • If the history can't be read (for example the file is locked by another process for more than 2 seconds), the signal is sent. Throttling never costs you an alert.

A signal no route matches still goes to console; that fallback is never suppressed.

docs.title: Dedup keys
docs.text:
Each signal's dedup key is the one the caller passed (dedup_key= in Python, dedup_key in the C JSON payload), or else a hash of its source, event_type, title and environment. Severity and message are not part of it, so a retry with a new error message is still the same incident. Pass your own key, such as the DAG and task id, when the title changes between retries.

A route that names a provider not configured under providers is a load-time error, as is a route with an empty providers list, an unknown mode, a dedup or rate_limit of zero, or an unknown key (so a typo such as mod: fanout fails at load time instead of leaving the route on failover). Unknown keys inside match are rejected too, so a typo such as enviroment: prod fails at load time instead of matching every signal.

docs.title: storage
docs.text:
Field Default Notes sink sqlite Only sqlite exists today. Postgres is on the roadmap. path ./signals.db Created if missing.

The SQLite file has two tables. signals holds one row per signal, with its overall delivery_status (pending, then delivered, partial or failed) and provider, the comma-separated providers that delivered it. deliveries holds one row per signal and provider, keyed by signal_id and provider: pending before the provider's first attempt, then delivered or failed, with its error and attempts. A process that exits in the middle of a fan-out therefore still shows which providers already have the signal. Databases created by earlier versions get the deliveries table the next time they are opened.

A third table, throttle, holds the recent sends of routes that set dedup or rate_limit. Rows older than a route's windows are deleted as it sends. Signals those settings held back are stored in signals with status skipped.

Every signal is written to the sink with its delivery status (delivered or failed), the provider that delivered it, and any error.

docs.title: Environment variables in values
docs.text:
${NAME} anywhere in a string value is replaced with the value of the environment variable NAME. Several placeholders can appear in one value.

  • An unset variable is a load-time error that names the variable. It is never silently replaced with an empty string.
  • Substitution happens after YAML parsing, so secrets that contain quotes, colons or newlines can't break the file's structure.

docs.title: Secrets from a secret store
docs.text:
A placeholder whose name has a colon reads a secret store instead of the environment. It works in any file of the chain, local or remote:

providers:
  slack:
    webhook_url: "${aws-sm:prod/opssignal#slack_url}"
  webhook:
    url: "${azure-kv:ops-vault/pagerduty-hook}"
Placeholder Reads Needs ${aws-sm:<name or ARN>} AWS Secrets Manager, current version opssignal[aws] ${gcp-sm:<project>/<secret>[/<version>]} GCP Secret Manager, latest unless pinned opssignal[gcp] ${azure-kv:<vault>/<name>[/<version>]} Azure Key Vault, current version unless pinned opssignal[azure]
  • #field at the end reads one field of a JSON secret, so one secret can hold several values (${aws-sm:prod/opssignal#slack_url}). Fields of one secret share one read.
  • A full ARN is read in its own region; a name is read in AWS_REGION. gcp-sm: also takes the full projects/<p>/secrets/<s>/versions/<v> form.
  • Credentials are the same chains as the cloud's config sources: IRSA, ECS and instance roles on AWS; workload identity, GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS and the metadata server on GCP; workload identity, a service principal and managed identity on Azure. The identity needs read access to the secret only (secretsmanager:GetSecretValue, roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor, or the Key Vault Secrets User role).
  • Endpoint overrides, for private endpoints, sovereign clouds and emulators: AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_SECRETSMANAGER, GOOGLE_SECRET_MANAGER_ENDPOINT, and AZURE_KEYVAULT_ENDPOINT with {vault} in it.

Rotation. Each reload checks the secrets as well as the files, so a rotated secret takes effect without a restart, within SIGNAL_SECRETS_TTL_SECS plus one reload interval.

Cost. Every store bills per read (about $0.05 per 10,000 on AWS, $0.03 on GCP and Azure). Values are kept in memory for SIGNAL_SECRETS_TTL_SECS, 300 by default, so each process reads each secret about 8,600 times a month instead of 43,000 at the 60-second reload interval. 0 reads on every reload.

Failures. A malformed reference, an unknown store, or a store whose extra isn't installed stops startup like any other config mistake. A store that can't be reached is treated like an unreachable remote file: at startup the client runs on the default config (console only) and picks the file up once the store answers; on reload the current config stays. Values are only held in memory. The config cache stores the file with its placeholders, never the secrets.

docs.title: Load-time errors
docs.text:
These all stop the config from loading, and the message says which rule failed:

  • invalid YAML
  • an unknown key anywhere in the file
  • an unset ${VAR}, or an unterminated or empty ${} placeholder
  • a ${store:...} secret reference that is malformed, names an unknown store, or needs an extra that isn't installed
  • a route that references an unconfigured provider, or lists no providers
  • a provider template with a syntax error, a part that provider doesn't have, or an unknown variable (see Message templates)
  • an extends that is not a path or a list of paths, forms a cycle, goes more than 8 files deep, or (from a remote file) names a local path
  • SIGNAL_CONFIG pointing at a path that is not a file, or using an unsupported URL scheme
  • SIGNAL_CONFIG_REFRESH_SECS that is not a whole number
  • a cloud URL whose support isn't installed (see Installing cloud support)

A remote source that can't be fetched is not on this list: it falls back as described in Remote configs.

docs.title: Python and Airflow
docs.text:
Install the package (it ships a compiled Rust extension):

pip install opssignal

To load signal.yaml from a cloud bucket, add the matching extra: opssignal[aws], opssignal[gcp] or opssignal[azure] (see Installing cloud support).

Note

The package is not published to PyPI yet. Until it is, build it from a checkout with uv sync --dev && (cd python && uv run --project .. maturin develop).

Send a signal directly:

from opssignal import notify

notify(
    source="airflow",
    event_type="task_failed",
    title="dbt model orders failed",
    severity="error",          # info | success | warning | error | critical
    message="relation does not exist",
    environment="prod",
)

Or drop the Airflow adapter into a DAG:

from opssignal.integrations.airflow import failure_callback

default_args = {
    "on_failure_callback": failure_callback,
}

notify() also takes the rest of the signal's context as keyword arguments: service, component, team, run_id, correlation_id, trace_id, log_url, dedup_key, and metadata (any JSON-serialisable object, usually a dict; dates and other values become strings).

notify() is fire-and-forget: it validates the input, hands the signal to a background runtime and returns immediately, so a slow Slack webhook never delays the task being monitored.

  • Invalid input (empty source, event_type or title) raises ValueError.
  • A broken signal.yaml raises RuntimeError on every call until it is fixed.
  • An unknown severity string falls back to info rather than raising.

Short-lived processes

Delivery happens in the background. Signals still in flight when the interpreter exits are flushed for up to 5 seconds; call opssignal.flush(timeout) to wait at a point of your choosing.

docs.title: dbt
docs.text:
Report a run's failures after any dbt command. dbt writes target/run_results.json on every run, so this works with dbt Core, dbt Fusion and artifacts downloaded from dbt Cloud, from a shell, CI job or orchestrator task:

dbt build; status=$?
python -m opssignal.integrations.dbt target/run_results.json --environment prod
exit $status

The reporter always exits 0, so the job still fails or passes on dbt's own status. From Python, call opssignal.integrations.dbt.report_run_results("target/run_results.json", environment="prod").

When dbt runs in-process (dbt-core 1.5+), pass the callback to dbtRunner to alert as each node fails, while the rest of the run continues:

from dbt.cli.main import dbtRunner
from opssignal.integrations.dbt import make_callback

dbtRunner(callbacks=[make_callback(environment="prod")]).invoke(["build"])

Both send one signal per failed node and per warned test:

dbt status Severity event_type Title error, fail error dbt_<resource>_failed, such as dbt_model_failed dbt model failed: orders warn warning dbt_<resource>_warned, such as dbt_test_warned dbt test warned: <test name>

service is the dbt project, component the node's unique_id, run_id the dbt invocation ID, and metadata holds the status, resource type, failure count, execution time, relation, dbt version, command and target. Skipped nodes are not reported: they were skipped because an upstream node failed, and that node has its own signal. The title is stable for a node, so a node that keeps failing run after run is deduplicated by providers that support it.

A broken source can fail hundreds of tests in one run. Past 20 signals (change it with --max-signals or max_signals=, 0 for no limit) the rest are rolled into one dbt_run_degraded signal that lists their IDs.

Route dbt signals like any other, for example:

routes:
  - match:
      source: dbt
      severity: [error]
      environment: prod
    providers: [pagerduty, slack]
  - match:
      source: dbt
      severity: [warning]
    providers: [slack]

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
cargo install --path crates/cli   # installs the `opssignal` binary
opssignal notify --source ci --event-type build_failed --severity error --title "main is red"

The CLI waits for delivery (up to 5 seconds) and exits non-zero if it fails. See CLI.

docs.title: No configuration needed
docs.text: With no signal.yaml, every signal goes to the console provider and is recorded in ./signals.db. Add a config file when you want Slack or webhooks; see Configuration.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: On Kubernetes, the routing rules go in a ConfigMap and the provider secrets go in a Secret. Every pod mounts the same ConfigMap, so one edit changes routing for every app in the namespace, and OpsSignal picks it up without a restart.

docs.title: 1. Routes in a ConfigMap
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: opssignal-config
data:
  signal.yaml: |
    providers:
      slack:
        webhook_url: "${SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL}"
    routes:
      - match:
          severity: [error, critical]
          environment: prod
        providers: [slack]
    storage:
      sink: sqlite
      path: /var/lib/opssignal/signals.db

The file holds no secrets. ${SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL} is filled in from each pod's environment when the config loads.

docs.title: 2. Secrets in a Secret
docs.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: opssignal-secrets
type: Opaque
stringData:
  SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL: "https://hooks.slack.com/services/..."

In practice this Secret usually comes from Vault, External Secrets or a sealed secret rather than being applied by hand.

docs.title: 3. Wire both into the Deployment
docs.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: my-service
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: my-service:latest
          env:
            - name: SIGNAL_CONFIG
              value: /etc/opssignal/signal.yaml
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: opssignal-secrets
          volumeMounts:
            - name: opssignal-config
              mountPath: /etc/opssignal
              readOnly: true
            - name: opssignal-data
              mountPath: /var/lib/opssignal
      volumes:
        - name: opssignal-config
          configMap:
            name: opssignal-config
        - name: opssignal-data
          emptyDir: {}

Mount the directory, not the file

Kubernetes never updates a ConfigMap mounted with subPath. Mount the whole ConfigMap as a directory, as above, or live reload will never see an edit.

docs.title: Changing the routes
docs.text:
Edit the ConfigMap:

kubectl edit configmap opssignal-config

The kubelet updates the mounted file within about a minute, and OpsSignal checks it every 60 seconds (SIGNAL_CONFIG_REFRESH_SECS), so a change reaches every pod in roughly two minutes with no restart. An edit that fails to load is logged and ignored, and the previous routes stay in place.

Two kinds of change still need a rollout (kubectl rollout restart deployment/my-service):

  • Secrets held in environment variables. Environment variables are fixed when a container starts, so a rotated Slack URL in the Secret reaches a pod only after it restarts. A ${aws-sm:...}, ${gcp-sm:...} or ${azure-kv:...} placeholder reads the secret store directly and picks up a rotation on its own (see Secrets from a secret store).
  • storage settings, which are never reloaded live.

docs.title: Rolling it out to every app
docs.text: A Helm chart or Kustomize component that adds the env, envFrom, volumeMounts and volumes blocks above lets every Deployment pick up OpsSignal without any app touching the config.

docs.title: A default per cluster, a file per team
docs.text:
A ConfigMap can hold several files. Keep the platform default and each team's file side by side, and point each service at its team's file, which extends the default:

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: opssignal-config
data:
  default.yaml: |
    providers:
      slack:
        webhook_url: "${ORG_SLACK_WEBHOOK}"
    routes:
      - match: { severity: [error, critical] }
        providers: [slack]
  payments.yaml: |
    extends: default.yaml
    routes:
      - match: { source: payments }
        providers: [slack]

env:
  - name: SIGNAL_CONFIG
    value: /etc/opssignal/payments.yaml

The default can also live in a bucket while team files stay in ConfigMaps: extends: s3://ops-config/prod/default.yaml.

docs.title: Across clusters: a config in a bucket
docs.text:
To share one config across clusters or with non-Kubernetes hosts, put signal.yaml in S3, GCS or Azure Blob Storage and point SIGNAL_CONFIG at it:

env:
  - name: SIGNAL_CONFIG
    value: s3://ops-config/prod/signal.yaml
  - name: AWS_REGION
    value: us-east-1

On AKS the equivalent is SIGNAL_CONFIG=az://ops-config/prod/signal.yaml with AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT_NAME set to the storage account. Python images need the matching extra, such as pip install 'opssignal[aws]'.

Give the pod's service account read access to that object through IRSA on EKS, or workload identity on GKE or AKS; no access keys are needed. See Remote configs for the cache and fallback behaviour.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
A provider delivers a signal to one destination. Configure each one under providers in signal.yaml, then name it in a route. Keep credentials out of the file with ${VAR} or a secret reference such as ${aws-sm:prod/opssignal#pd_key} (see Configuration).

Provider Key Required fields Optional fields Console console none enabled Slack slack webhook_url none Webhook webhook url none PagerDuty pagerduty routing_key url Microsoft Teams teams webhook_url none Opsgenie opsgenie api_key url, tags Email email from, to, and smtp.host or ses cc, subject_prefix, smtp.port, smtp.username, smtp.password, smtp.tls, ses.region, ses.configuration_set

Added in v1.0.0-beta.2

Every provider also takes an optional template block that replaces parts of its message with your own text. See Message templates.

All providers are in the base package. The one exception is email through the Amazon SES API, which needs opssignal[aws]; email over SMTP, SES's SMTP endpoint included, needs no extra.

By default a route's providers are tried in order and delivery stops at the first one that succeeds, so later providers are fallbacks, not extra copies. A route providers: [pagerduty, teams] pages through PagerDuty and posts to Teams only if PagerDuty could not be reached. Add mode: fanout to send to every provider of the route at once instead; see delivery modes. Any non-2xx response or connection error is a failed attempt; each provider gets up to 3 attempts with backoff.

docs.title: Console
docs.text: Prints one line per signal to stdout. It is always registered, because unmatched signals fall back to it, and cannot be turned off.

docs.title: Slack
docs.text:
providers:
  slack:
    webhook_url: "${SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL}"

Posts the title, message and a severity emoji to a Slack incoming webhook.

docs.title: Webhook
docs.text:
providers:
  webhook:
    url: "https://alerts.example.com/opssignal"

POSTs the full signal as JSON, with every field of the signal model.

docs.title: PagerDuty
docs.text:
providers:
  pagerduty:
    routing_key: "${PAGERDUTY_ROUTING_KEY}"
    # EU-hosted accounts only:
    # url: "https://events.eu.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue"

routes:
  - match:
      severity: [critical]
      environment: prod
    providers: [pagerduty, slack]

Triggers an alert through the Events API v2. routing_key is the integration key of an Events API v2 integration on a PagerDuty service (Service > Integrations > Add integration). url defaults to https://events.pagerduty.com/v2/enqueue.

How a signal maps to the event:

PagerDuty field From the signal dedup_key dedup_key (the core computes one from source, event type, title and environment if the caller gives none), cut to 255 characters payload.summary title, cut to 1024 characters payload.source source payload.severity severity; success becomes info payload.timestamp timestamp payload.component component, if set payload.group service, if set payload.class event_type payload.custom_details signal_id, event_type, severity, and whichever of message, environment, team, run_id, correlation_id, trace_id and metadata are set links log_url, if set, as "Logs"

Because the dedup key is stable, the same failure sent again adds to the open alert instead of paging a second time. OpsSignal only triggers alerts; it does not acknowledge or resolve them.

Route only the severities that should wake someone to PagerDuty. A route that sends info signals there will page on them.

docs.title: Microsoft Teams
docs.text:
providers:
  teams:
    webhook_url: "${TEAMS_WEBHOOK_URL}"

routes:
  - match:
      severity: [warning, error]
    providers: [teams]

Posts an Adaptive Card to a Teams channel. Create the URL with the Workflows app: in the channel, choose Workflows > Post to a channel when a webhook request is received, and copy the URL it gives you. Legacy Office 365 connector incoming-webhook URLs accept the same message, but Microsoft is retiring them.

The card shows:

  • the title, coloured by severity (red for error and critical, amber for warning, green for success);
  • the message, if set;
  • facts for severity, source and event type, plus environment, service, component, team and run ID when set;
  • a View logs button when log_url is set.

docs.title: Opsgenie
docs.text:
providers:
  opsgenie:
    api_key: "${OPSGENIE_API_KEY}"
    # EU-hosted accounts only:
    # url: "https://api.eu.opsgenie.com/v2/alerts"
    tags: [data-platform]

routes:
  - match:
      severity: [critical, error]
      environment: prod
    providers: [opsgenie, slack]

Creates an alert through the Alert API. api_key is the key of an API integration on the Opsgenie team that should receive the alert (Teams > your team > Integrations > Add integration > API). The team's routing rules and escalations decide who is notified. url defaults to https://api.opsgenie.com/v2/alerts.

How a signal maps to the alert:

Opsgenie field From the signal message title, cut to 130 characters alias dedup_key, cut to 512 characters description message, followed by a "Logs:" line when log_url is set priority severity: critical is P1, error P2, warning P3, info and success P5 source source entity service/component, or whichever of the two is set tags the configured tags, then the severity and the environment, up to 20 details signal_id, event_type, severity, timestamp, whichever of environment, service, component, team, run_id, correlation_id, trace_id and log_url are set, and each top-level metadata key as metadata.<key>

Because the alias is stable, the same failure sent again raises the open alert's count instead of opening a second alert. OpsSignal only creates alerts; it does not acknowledge or close them.

Atlassian is folding Opsgenie into Jira Service Management. Its operations alert API takes the same request, so a migrated team can point url at the endpoint shown on its JSM API integration and keep the rest of the config.

docs.title: Email
docs.text:
providers:
  email:
    from: "OpsSignal <alerts@example.com>"
    to: [data-oncall@example.com]
    cc: [data-platform@example.com]     # optional
    subject_prefix: "[opssignal]"       # optional
    smtp:
      host: smtp.example.com
      username: "${SMTP_USERNAME}"
      password: "${SMTP_PASSWORD}"
      # tls: starttls (default, port 587) | tls (port 465) | none (port 25)
      # port: 2587

routes:
  - match:
      severity: [error, critical]
    providers: [slack, email]

Sends a plain-text email through any SMTP server, or through the Amazon SES API with ses in place of smtp. The subject is <subject_prefix> [SEVERITY] <title>; the body has the message, the signal's fields (severity, source, event, environment, service, component, team, run ID, correlation and trace IDs, log URL), its metadata, and the signal ID and time.

tls decides how the connection is secured:

tls Default port Meaning starttls 587 Plain connection upgraded with STARTTLS. If the server doesn't offer it, the send fails rather than going out unencrypted. tls 465 TLS from the first byte (SMTPS). none 25 No encryption. Only for a relay on localhost or inside your network.

username and password go together; leave both out for a relay that does not ask for authentication. Addresses are checked when the config loads, so a typo fails at startup instead of on the first alert.

Every email for the same dedup_key carries the same References header and subject, so mail clients thread repeats of a failure into one conversation.

Hosted email services all accept SMTP, so they need no extra package:

Service smtp.host Credentials Amazon SES email-smtp.<region>.amazonaws.com SES SMTP credentials (SES console > SMTP settings) SendGrid smtp.sendgrid.net username apikey, password the API key Mailgun smtp.mailgun.org (smtp.eu.mailgun.org in the EU) the domain's SMTP login Postmark smtp.postmarkapp.com the server API token as both username and password Gmail / Google Workspace smtp.gmail.com the account and an app password, or use the Workspace SMTP relay Microsoft 365 smtp.office365.com a mailbox with SMTP AUTH enabled

docs.title: Amazon SES API
docs.text:
providers:
  email:
    from: "OpsSignal <alerts@example.com>"
    to: [data-oncall@example.com]
    ses:
      region: eu-west-1               # optional; defaults to AWS_REGION
      configuration_set: alerts       # optional

Sends through the SES v2 SendEmail API with the standard AWS credential chain: an EKS service account (IRSA), an ECS task role, an EC2 instance profile, or AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. There are no SMTP credentials to store or rotate. The role needs ses:SendEmail on the sending identity, and from must be an address or domain verified in SES for that region (while the account is in the SES sandbox, so must every recipient). AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_SESV2 overrides the endpoint, for a VPC endpoint or LocalStack.

This needs AWS support: pip install 'opssignal[aws]' for Python, or a CLI or C library built with --features aws. Without it, the config fails to load with an error naming the extra, rather than failing on the first alert. Set exactly one of smtp and ses. The message is the same one SMTP sends, threading headers included.

Email is a slow channel: use it for the trail and for people who are not on chat, and pair it with an on-call provider for anything urgent. On a failover route, [email, slack] sends to Slack only when the email could not be handed to the server; use mode: fanout to send both.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The Rust API of opssignal-core is generated with cargo doc and published with this site:

Open the opssignal-core API reference

The reference matches the docs version picked at the top of the page.

The parts most callers need:

Item Purpose SignalClient::from_env() Build a client from the discovered config. SignalClient::from_config(&Config) Build a client from a config you loaded yourself. SignalClient::notify_async(SignalInput) Fire-and-forget delivery. The signal is saved as pending before this returns. SignalClient::flush(Duration) Wait for fire-and-forget deliveries to finish. Dropping the client does this for up to 5 seconds. SignalClient::notify_sync(SignalInput, Duration) Blocking delivery with a timeout. Returns a DeliveryResult, whose deliveries lists each provider's outcome. routing::DeliveryMode A route's mode: Failover (default) or Fanout. config::Config::{discover, from_file, from_yaml_str} Load signal.yaml. delivery::Provider Trait to implement for a new provider. sink::SignalSink Trait to implement for a new sink.

The Python API is opssignal.notify() and opssignal.flush(timeout=5.0), plus the Airflow adapter; see Getting started. The package flushes on interpreter exit by itself.

The C library exports signal_notify_async(json), signal_flush(timeout_ms) and signal_free_string(ptr). Call signal_flush before the host exits, or signals still being delivered are cut off (they stay recorded as pending).

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
One tag publishes everything. .github/workflows/release.yml builds the packages below, tests the wheels, then uploads them.

Registry Package Built from Installed with PyPI opssignal python/ + crates/python pip install opssignal PyPI opssignal-aws python/addons/aws + crates/python-aws pip install 'opssignal[aws]' PyPI opssignal-gcp python/addons/gcp + crates/python-gcp pip install 'opssignal[gcp]' PyPI opssignal-azure python/addons/azure + crates/python-azure pip install 'opssignal[azure]' crates.io opssignal-core crates/core cargo add opssignal-core crates.io opssignal-cli crates/cli cargo install opssignal-cli

opssignal[all] installs all three add-ons. opssignal-ffi and the opssignal-py* crates are publish = false: the Python crates only exist inside wheels, and C users build the library from source.

Wheels are abi3, so one wheel per platform covers CPython 3.9 and later: Linux x86_64 and aarch64 (manylinux and musllinux), Windows x86_64 and macOS arm64 (Apple Silicon). Each package also gets an sdist. Intel Macs have no wheel, because macOS runner minutes bill at 10x; there pip builds from the sdist, which needs a Rust toolchain. To ship Intel Mac wheels, uncomment the macos-x86_64 line in the wheels matrix in release.yml.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text: Nothing is published until this is done. PyPI needs no stored secret at all; crates.io needs a token for the first release only.

docs.title: GitHub environments
docs.text: In Settings > Environments, create five environments: pypi, pypi-aws, pypi-gcp, pypi-azure and crates-io. Add yourself as a required reviewer on each, so a pushed tag waits for your click before anything is uploaded (the Actions run lets you approve them all at once).

docs.title: Docs site
docs.text:
The docs are published by .github/workflows/docs.yml to the gh-pages branch, one copy per version (built with mike). The first run creates the branch. Then, in Settings > Pages, set Source to Deploy from a branch, branch gh-pages, folder / (root).

To publish docs for a tag that was cut before versioned docs existed, run Actions > Docs > Run workflow on main with that tag, for example v1.0.0-beta.1.

docs.title: PyPI: trusted publishing
docs.text:
The projects don't exist yet, so register a pending publisher for each one at https://pypi.org/manage/account/publishing/ (do the same on https://test.pypi.org if you want a rehearsal). Add four entries, one per project, each with its own environment name:

PyPI project name Environment name opssignal pypi opssignal-aws pypi-aws opssignal-gcp pypi-gcp opssignal-azure pypi-azure

All four use owner adithyapathipaka, repository OpsSignal and workflow release.yml. The environments must differ: a trusted-publishing token can create only the one project whose pending publisher it matched, so four publishers with the same environment fail with "Non-user identities cannot create new projects".

A pending publisher does not reserve the name: whoever uploads first gets it. The first successful release turns each one into a normal publisher.

docs.title: crates.io: token first, then trusted publishing
docs.text:
crates.io only allows trusted publishing for crates that already exist.

  1. Sign in to https://crates.io with GitHub and verify your email address (publishing is refused without it).
  2. Create an API token at https://crates.io/settings/tokens with the publish-new and publish-update scopes, limited to the crates opssignal-core and opssignal-cli, with a short expiry.
  3. Save it as the secret CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN on the crates-io environment.
  4. After the first release, open each crate's Settings > Trusted Publishing on crates.io and add owner adithyapathipaka, repository OpsSignal, workflow release.yml, environment crates-io. Then delete the CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN secret and revoke the token; the workflow switches to trusted publishing on its own when the secret is gone.

docs.title: Cutting a release
docs.text:
1. Open a PR that turns ## [Unreleased] in CHANGELOG.md into ## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD, adds a fresh empty ## [Unreleased] above it, updates the compare links at the bottom, and checks that every "Added in" note in docs/ names this version. Merge it, so the tagged commit's docs and changelog match the release.

That section becomes the GitHub release notes: the workflow runs scripts/release_notes.py, which adds install commands, the docs link and a compare link to the previous tag. Write it for users (what they get, what changed, what to watch for), not as a list of PRs. A tag with no matching ## [X.Y.Z] section stops the run before it builds.

  1. Tag the commit on main you want to release and push the tag:

    git tag v0.2.0
git push origin v0.2.0

    The tag sets the version. Before building, the workflow runs scripts/set_version.py to write 0.2.0 into Cargo.toml ([workspace.package] and the opssignal-core pin in crates/cli), the four pyproject.toml files, the extras pins in python/pyproject.toml, and opssignal.__version__. It also points the docs links PyPI shows (each package's Documentation URL and README) at that version's docs, for example https://adithyapathipaka.github.io/OpsSignal/0.2.0/. Then scripts/check_versions.py confirms they all agree. You don't need a version-bump commit.

    Tags are vX.Y.Z for a release, or vX.Y.Z-alpha.N, -beta.N or -rc.N for a pre-release; anything else stops the run before it builds. A pre-release keeps that form on crates.io (1.0.0-beta.1) and uses Python's spelling on PyPI (1.0.0b1). Neither registry gives it to users by default: they ask for it with pip install --pre opssignal or opssignal-core = "1.0.0-beta.1". The GitHub release is marked as a pre-release.

    The change is made only inside the release run. The files on main keep their old version, so main doesn't show which version was last released; the tags do.

  2. Approve the pypi-aws, pypi-gcp, pypi-azure, pypi and crates-io deployments in the Actions run.

The run uploads the three add-ons first, then opssignal (its extras pin the add-ons, so they must exist first), then opssignal-core and opssignal-cli, and finally creates a GitHub release with every wheel and sdist attached.

The same tag also publishes that version's docs: the site gets a X.Y.Z (or X.Y.Z-beta.N) entry in its version picker, and if it is the highest tag, latest (what the site's home page opens) moves to it. Merges to main keep updating the dev version. This needs no approval.

To build and test everything without publishing, run the workflow by hand from Actions > Release > Run workflow. Pull requests don't run it, to save Actions minutes, so do this before tagging if a change touched the packaging (a pyproject.toml, Cargo.toml or release.yml); otherwise a packaging mistake only shows up when the tag runs, and stops it before anything is uploaded.

docs.title: If a release fails halfway
docs.text:
Registry uploads can't be undone, and a version number can never be reused on either registry, even after it is yanked or deleted.

  • Before any upload (a build or smoke test failed): fix it, delete the tag, and tag again.
  • After some uploads: use Re-run failed jobs on the same run. Both publish jobs skip anything already uploaded, so a re-run picks up where it stopped. If the fix needs a code change, tag the next patch version and release that instead. Yank a broken version with cargo yank or PyPI's Yank button rather than deleting it.

docs.title: Message templates
docs.text:
Added in v1.0.0-beta.2

Providers take a template block that reshapes the message they send.

Every provider has a built-in message format. A template block under a provider replaces parts of that message with your own text, written in Jinja syntax:

providers:
  slack:
    webhook_url: "${SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL}"
    template:
      text: |
        {{ emoji }} *[{{ environment | default("no env") | upper }}] {{ title }}*
        {% if message %}{{ message }}{% endif %}
        {% if log_url %}<{{ log_url }}|View logs>{% endif %}
  pagerduty:
    routing_key: "${PD_ROUTING_KEY}"
    template:
      summary: "[{{ service }}] {{ title }}"

Templates are set per provider, and only the parts you set change. A provider without a template block, or a part a template doesn't set, keeps the built-in format, so existing configs send exactly what they did before.

docs.title: Parts you can template
docs.text:
Provider Parts Replaces Extra variables console text The printed line. slack text The message text. emoji: the severity's Slack emoji, such as :x: webhook body The whole JSON body. Must render to valid JSON; see Webhook bodies. pagerduty summary payload.summary. Cut to PagerDuty's 1024 characters. teams title, text The card's title and message text blocks. The fact table and log button stay. opsgenie message, description The alert message (cut to 130 characters) and description (cut to 15000). email subject, body The subject (after subject_prefix, which still applies) and the plain-text body. A subject is joined onto one line.

Everything else a provider sends stays as the built-in format: PagerDuty's dedup_key, severity and custom details, Opsgenie's alias, priority and tags, email threading headers. That keeps deduplication and routing on the receiving side working whatever the text says.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Every template sees the signal's fields by name:

Variable Notes title, source, event_type, severity Always set. severity is lowercase: info, success, warning, error, critical. message, environment, service, component, team, run_id, correlation_id, trace_id, log_url, dedup_key Undefined when the signal doesn't set them, so {% if message %} works and {{ message }} prints nothing. metadata The signal's metadata object, such as {{ metadata.dag_id }}. Loop over it with the items filter. id, timestamp The signal id, and the time it was created as RFC 3339 in UTC.

Filters and tests from Jinja's built-in set work, such as upper, lower, default, replace, trim, join, length and tojson.

docs.title: Mistakes stop the load
docs.text:
A template is checked when the config loads, like the rest of the file. These are load-time errors, with the key that failed in the message:

  • a syntax error ({{ title)
  • a part the provider doesn't have (providers.slack.template.txt)
  • a variable that doesn't exist ({{ tittle }}), including another provider's extra variable (emoji outside Slack)

metadata.<key> is not checked, since metadata differs from signal to signal.

docs.title: A template never costs the alert
docs.text: If a template still fails while a signal is sent (for example, {{ metadata.count + 1 }} on a signal whose count is text), or renders to nothing but whitespace, the provider logs a warning and sends its built-in format instead. The alert goes out either way.

docs.title: Webhook bodies
docs.text:
The webhook body template must produce JSON. Use the tojson filter for every value, so quotes and newlines in a title are escaped:

providers:
  webhook:
    url: "https://alerts.example.com/hook"
    template:
      body: |
        {
          "summary": {{ title | tojson }},
          "level": {{ severity | upper | tojson }},
          "labels": {"env": {{ environment | default("none") | tojson }}}
        }

A body that is not valid JSON once rendered is logged, and the full signal is sent instead, as without a template.

docs.title: Escaping
docs.text: Templates don't escape anything. Slack and Teams render their own markdown, so a * or _ in a title formats text there, as it does with the built-in format.

docs.title: Templates and layered configs
docs.text:
template belongs to its provider entry, and a later layer replaces a provider entry whole. A team file that wants its own Slack text restates the provider:

# teams/data-platform.yaml
extends: ../default.yaml
providers:
  slack:
    webhook_url: "${DATA_SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL}"
    template:
      text: "{{ emoji }} [data-platform] {{ title }}"

docs.title: Checking a template
docs.text:
opssignal preview prints what each provider would be sent for a signal, without sending or recording anything:

opssignal preview --config signal.yaml \
  --source airflow --event-type task_failed --severity error \
  --title "load failed" --environment prod --metadata '{"dag_id": "orders"}'

docs.title: Python and C
docs.text: Templates live in the config, so the Python package and the C library use them with no code changes.
